summary: This memo defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP). It adds managed objects and textual conventions for tunnels, identifiers, and Label Switching Router information so network management tools can handle them.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a list of meters and switches that lets people watch and control special network tunnels, using the same kind of tools they use for other equipment.

which mib modules does rfc 7453 define
subtitle: Four SNMP MIB modules that let management tools handle MPLS-TP tunnels, including bidirectional ones and non-IP node identifiers.

tldr.problem: The existing MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineering MIBs cover only some tunnel types and identify endpoints only by IP address, which is not enough for MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) tunnels.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7453 defines four MIB modules that sparsely extend the existing tunnel and cross-connect tables, plus a node configuration table that maps non-IP node identifiers to local numbers.
tldr.outcome: Together with RFC 3812 and RFC 3813, the modules cover all six combinations of static or dynamic with unidirectional, associated bidirectional or co-routed bidirectional tunnels.

today: RFC 7453 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2015. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 7453 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols. It adds textual conventions and managed objects for tunnels, identifiers and Label Switching Routers (LSRs), to support MPLS MIB modules for transport networks. The modules extend existing MPLS MIB objects so that they support the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) and other MPLS networks, which is why "MPLS-TP" is not in the module names.

The RFC uses the Internet-Standard Management Framework. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and defined using SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579, RFC 2580).

The RFC notes that SNMP SET is no longer recommended for configuring MPLS networks. Some objects are still read-write or read-create so the extensions stay consistent with the base tables in RFC 3812.
sections.plainLanguage: Network devices keep a list of meters and settings that a management program can read. This document adds more entries to that list for a special kind of tunnel.

sections.title: Why the Existing MIBs Were Not Enough
sections.content:
Three kinds of point-to-point MPLS tunnel may be built between LSRs A and B. A unidirectional tunnel has a single LSP. An associated bidirectional tunnel has two separately routed LSPs, one each way, that together form one logical transport path. A co-routed bidirectional tunnel is an associated one where the return LSP follows the reverse of the forward path, in both nodes and links. Any of these may be configured statically or created dynamically by an LSP management protocol.

The MPLS TE MIB (RFC 3812) and the GMPLS TE MIB (RFC 4802) address only a subset of those combinations, and they are limited to two endpoint LSRs identified by IP addresses. MPLS-TP tunnels are bidirectional by nature and may use non-IP identifiers for their endpoints. Because most attributes of MPLS-TE tunnels also apply to MPLS-TP tunnels, the RFC chose to reuse and extend the existing MIB definitions instead of defining a new one.
sections.plainLanguage: The old control panel could only describe some kinds of tunnels, and only by their street address. The new panel handles two-way tunnels and other kinds of names.

sections.title: The Four MIB Modules
sections.content:
The RFC defines four modules, used together with the modules of RFC 3812 and RFC 3813. They are defined in this one document because all are needed for MPLS-TP.

  • MPLS-TC-EXT-STD-MIB: textual conventions for LSPs of MPLS-based transport networks.
  • MPLS-ID-STD-MIB: identifier objects for MPLS traffic engineering in transport networks.
  • MPLS-LSR-EXT-STD-MIB: generic objects for LSRs in transport networks, including the mplsXCExtTable, which sparsely extends mplsXCTable and points back to the tunnel entry.
  • MPLS-TE-EXT-STD-MIB: the tunnel extensions, described in the next section.

All the new modules depend on MPLS-TC-EXT-STD-MIB. The ID and TE extension modules reference objects in MPLS-TE-STD-MIB, and the LSR extension module references MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB. An MPLS-TP tunnel can be configured as an interface, using the same ifType 150 as RFC 3812, and the existing mplsTunnelTable is reused for MPLS-TP tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four new pages added to the big instruction binder. One has shared word definitions, one has names, one is for routers and one is for tunnels.

sections.title: Tunnel Tables and Local Identifiers
sections.content:
The existing mplsTunnelTable is indexed by tunnel index, instance, ingress LSR ID and egress LSR ID, so MPLS-TP identifiers cannot be used directly. The mplsTunnelExtNodeConfigTable solves this by assigning a local identifier to each Global_ID::Node_ID or ICC_Operator_ID::Node_ID. In the IP-compatible mode, the local identifier must lie in the range 0 to 16777215, below 16777216 (1.0.0.0), the first valid IP address, so it can stand in as the LSR ID.

Two read-only tables, mplsTunnelExtNodeIpMapTable and mplsTunnelExtNodeIccMapTable, look up the local identifier for a given Global_ID::Node_ID or ICC_Operator_ID::Node_ID. The CC is two uppercase letters and the ICC is one to six uppercase letters or digits, encoded with T.50 as in RFC 6370.

The mplsTunnelExtTable sparsely extends mplsTunnelTable with MPLS-TP objects. Its RowPointer mplsTunnelExtOppositeDirPtr points to the tunnel entry in the opposite direction. In mplsXCExtTable, mplsXCExtTunnelPointer is a read-only back pointer to the tunnel and mplsXCExtOppositeDirXCPtr points to the opposite-direction XC entry. A pointer value of zeroDotZero means no entry is associated.
sections.plainLanguage: The old tunnel list only understood house numbers. This adds a phone book that turns other kinds of names into simple numbers the old list can use.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Section 9 of the RFC walks through setting up MPLS-TP bidirectional tunnels with IP tunnel identifiers between East and West: a static co-routed bidirectional tunnel, a static associated bidirectional tunnel and a signaled co-routed bidirectional tunnel. Only objects relevant to MPLS-TP are shown, and the RFC says the examples indicate how MIB values would be returned if the circumstances were configured by other means.

The first step creates two rows in mplsTunnelExtNodeConfigTable, one for the ingress and one for the egress node. The example uses local identifiers 1 and 2, Global_ID 1234 and Node_IDs 10 and 20. The read-only IP map table is then populated automatically. The tunnel rows then use those local numbers as mplsTunnelIngressLSRId and mplsTunnelEgressLSRId, and the examples go on to fill in the tunnel, segment and cross-connect entries from RFC 3812 and RFC 3813.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are fill-in-the-form demos. First you register the two end points, then you fill in the tunnel form using their new numbers.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC follows the security considerations of Section 12 of RFC 3812. Write access to mplsIdGlobalId, mplsIdNodeId, mplsIdCc and mplsIdIcc could let wrong values confuse OAM functions, or let one node impersonate another. The tunnel extension tables collectively provision MPLS-TP tunnels and also reveal the tunnel topology, so they may be sensitive.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features, and deploying SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must configure access so only legitimate principals can read or change the objects.

IANA assigned four object identifiers under the mplsStdMIB subtree: 17 for MPLS-TC-EXT-STD-MIB, 18 for MPLS-ID-STD-MIB, 19 for MPLS-LSR-EXT-STD-MIB and 20 for MPLS-TE-EXT-STD-MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: The control panel can show how the network is wired, and a wrong setting could confuse things. So only trusted people should get the keys.

items.title: Unidirectional
items.text: A single LSP from A to B.

items.title: Associated bidirectional
items.text: Two separately routed LSPs, one each way, forming one logical path.

items.title: Co-routed bidirectional
items.text: The B to A LSP follows the reverse of the A to B path, in nodes and links.
